ola-en-01-tip.caption:
We try to file weeks before the deadline rather than on it. That is not keenness. It is room.

When a return goes in early and something looks odd in the figures, a payment that appears twice, a cost nobody can place, a bank line that does not match the invoice, there is time to ask you about it, time for you to find the answer, and time to put it right before anything is submitted. Do that same piece of work on the last evening of January and the odd figure becomes a decision made at speed. Usually the cautious one. Usually the one that costs you something.

So we start earlier than most people expect us to. You will hear from us in the autumn about the year that ended in April, and we will ask our awkward questions while they are still easy to answer. By the time the deadline comes round, your return has often been filed for weeks and the only thing left is to pay what it says.

Our offices are in Luton and Birmingham. The first conversation is free and lasts thirty minutes.

ola-en-01-tip.title: We file early so questions still have time

ola-en-02-acq.caption:
Most people who want to change accountant put it off, because they picture a project. Chasing their own records. Explaining themselves twice. Having an awkward conversation with somebody they have known for years.

You do not make that call. We do, in writing, and firms expect it: one accountant asking another whether there is anything we ought to know before we take you on, and asking for your papers at the same time. Your old accountant has written the same letter about somebody else's client. It is a normal piece of correspondence between two firms, not a complaint about either of you.

What we ask for is specific, because vague requests come back half answered: the last set of accounts, the tax computations behind them, your figures for the year in progress, the references that let us act for you with HMRC, and anything still open. Then we chase it, because letters sit in inboxes for weeks. You hear from us when the papers land and, more usefully, if something is missing and we need to go back for it.

None of it needs a date in your diary. It happens between two offices while you get on with the work, and the first you need to think about it again is when we tell you we have everything.

Luton and Birmingham. The first conversation is free and lasts thirty minutes, and you are welcome to bring your questions rather than your paperwork.
ola-en-02-acq.ask: Send this to anyone who has been meaning to move accountant for a year.
ola-en-02-acq.title: Moving accountant takes one signature

ola-en-03-acq.caption:
A lender wants three years of figures by Friday. A new landlord wants your last accounts. Somebody asks for the invoice behind one line in a year you have half forgotten. These requests never arrive at a convenient moment, and they are the moment you find out how your paperwork is really kept.

Ours is kept so that the answer is an email. We work from scans, named and sorted by year as they come in, so nothing depends on one carrier bag surviving a house move. You can ask us for a copy of anything we hold for you, and it is yours to keep whether you stay with us or not.

It also matters when things go wrong. If records are lost, stolen or destroyed and genuinely cannot be replaced, a return can be filed on estimated or provisional figures, with HMRC told which you have used and the real ones followed up afterwards. That is a workable position, but it is a worse one than simply having the papers. Most of the work of avoiding it happens quietly, months earlier, in how the filing is done.

Offices in Luton and Birmingham, and the first conversation is free and lasts thirty minutes.
ola-en-03-acq.ask: Save this for the next time someone asks you for an old year's figures.
ola-en-03-acq.title: Your records, scanned and still yours

ola-en-04-joke.caption:
Everyone has one customer like this, and you already know which one of yours it is.

The quieter part is what you can show about it. Three months of phone calls live in your memory, where they are no use to anyone. The same three calls written down, with the date next to each one, sit beside the invoice in your records and stay there. So write the note when you put the phone down: who you spoke to, what they promised, when they said it would happen. It takes a line.

That note is worth having whichever way the invoice goes. If the money arrives, you have the history of how long it took, which is useful the next time that customer asks for credit. If it never arrives, you are not trying to reconstruct a year from memory when we sit down and go through it with you.

Bring the list if a few of these are sitting on your books. Luton or Birmingham, and the first conversation is free and lasts thirty minutes.

ola-en-04-joke.title: The cheque that has been in the post since August

ola-en-05-quote.caption:
Nothing of any size arrives all at once, and Epictetus reached for fruit to say so: the grape and the fig take the time they take.

A business behaves the same way. The first year is often all cost and little comfort. The second can look like standing still, except that the work done in the first is quietly setting underneath it. This is where figures earn their keep, because they see what a single month cannot. A slow year with a rising trend is a different animal from a slow year with a falling one, and only the records tell you which one you are standing in.

The passage is from the Discourses, Book I, chapter 15, and it was an answer to someone who wanted a result immediately. First the blossom, then the fruit, then the ripening, and none of it can be hurried along by wanting it more.

Worth keeping in mind during the quiet weeks after Christmas, when trade goes flat and it starts to feel personal. It usually is not personal. It is January.

Luton and Birmingham, if you would like someone to go through the figures with you.
